name: Dijon
lede: Dijon is a mustard-toned yellow-green named for a Burgundy city; the color books are silent on it, but the city shows up in them for a different reason, as the place where zinc white was worked out.

sections.title: A city's name
sections.body:
Dijon is a city in Burgundy, and as a color name it points to the mustardy yellow-green of this swatch [4]. None of the color books consulted for this site discusses Dijon as a color [4]. The earliest record of the name in our sources is the 2010 xkcd color survey, so the link to the city's mustard is the likely origin, not a documented one [4]. In printed English the adjective peaks in the 1980s [4]. Its closest relatives among named colors are [[mustard]] and [[chartreuse]], with [[olive]] on the greener side [4].

In the archive it is rare: 5 paintings, 0.02 percent of 23,781, rarer than 73 percent of named colors [4]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so the match is to a look, not a pigment [4].

sections.title: The Dijon Academy and zinc white
sections.body:
The city appears in the books through its academy. Lead white was a poison and darkened in sulphurous air, so in the 1780s the French government asked the chemist Guyton de Morveau for a safer white [1]. His 1782 report named zinc oxide, as the best candidate, and credited its synthesis to Courtois, a laboratory demonstrator at the Dijon Academy [1][3]. Compare [[white]] and [[ghost-white]].

Zinc white was nontoxic and did not blacken [1]. It was also less opaque, slow to dry in oil and about four times the price of lead white [3]. The books are not sure who deserves the credit: one pigment reference says it is unclear whether the first production belongs to Courtois or to Guyton de Morveau [2]. Another describes Courtois as a science demonstrator at the Academy and Guyton as a magistrate who became one of France's most inventive chemists [5].

questions.q: What did Guyton de Morveau report in 1782 about zinc oxide?
choices: It was the best candidate to replace lead white
It was the best new red
It was a source of purple
questions.answer: It was the best candidate to replace lead white

questions.q: Why was zinc white not an instant success, according to the books?
choices: It was less opaque, slow to dry and costly
It turned black in sulphurous air
It was only made in Italy
questions.answer: It was less opaque, slow to dry and costly

openers: The Dijon Academy is where zinc white, the safer replacement for lead white, was worked out in the 1780s.
